full_judgment:
Md. Ruhul Quddus, J: The above noted three criminal appeals arising out of one proceeding have been heard analogously and are disposed of by this judgment. Of them Criminal Appeal No. 173 of 1992 under section 10 of the Criminal Law Amendment Act, 1958 (Act XL of 1958) is directed against the judgment order dated 03.02.1992 passed by the Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka in Special Case No.07 of 1991 arising out of Cantonment Police Station Case No.4 dated 08.01.1991 convicting the accused under section 5(2) read with section 5(1)(e) of the Prevention of Corruption Act, 1947 ( Act II of 1947) and sentencing him thereunder to suffer simple imprisonment for three years and confiscating an amount of Taka 1,90,81,565/- with a Toyota Land Cruiser 11 Jeep to the State, while acquitted him of the charge under section 5(1) (c) of the Act II of 1947 read with section 5 (2) thereof. The Government Appeal No. 5 of 1992 under section 417 (1) (a) and 417 A (1) of the Code of Criminal Procedure is directed against inadequacy of sentence as well as acquittal in the selfsame judgment and order, while Government Appeal No. 6 of 1992 under section 476B of the Code is directed against the post-judgment order dated 03.02.1992 passed in the selfsame proceeding rejecting an application filed by the Public Prosecutor under section 476 thereof for lodging a complaint against DW 1 Tajul Islam Chowdhury (respondent in the appeal). 

 53. After closing the prosecution evidence the accused was examined under section 342 of the Code to which lie reiterated his innocence and took the plea that the money in question was collected from the members and leaders of Jatio Party by selling money receipts. The money belonged to the party and he possessed the same as its Chairman and it was kept for purchasing an office building at Dhanmandi. A suit for realization of the money was pending before the 3rd  Court of Subordinate Judge (now Joint District Judge), Dhaka wherein he himself as well as the Government was made defendants. He produced a certified copy of the plaint in the said suit. 

 54. The defence also examined 10 witnesses. Of them DW 1 Tajul Islam Chowdhury, a lawyer and Member of Parliament from Kurigram-2 constituency (respondent in Govt. Appeal No.6 of 1992) stated that he was the Office Secretary of Jatio Party. Their office was housed at Road No. 3, Dhanmandi, which was an abandoned property. Since its formation in 1986, Jatio Party possessed the house as its office taking lease from the Government. In its meeting held on 10.07.1990, the Central Committee of Jatio Party decided to raise a fund for purchasing its permanent office building. Accordingly, they printed one and half lac money receipt-books each containing one hundred leafs. On receipt of advance payment, the books were distributed to the 

 59. The convict Hussian Mohammad Ershad preferred Criminal Appeal No.173 of 1992 challenging the judgment and order of conviction and sentence, while the Government preferred Government Appeal No.05 of 1992 against inadequacy of sentence awarded upon the accused-appellant under section 5(1)(e) of the Act 11 of 1947 and also against acquittal of charge under section 5(1)(c) of the Act. The Government preferred another appeal being Government Appeal No.06 of 1992 against order dated 03.02.1992 rejecting the application filed by the Public Prosecutor for initiation of a proceeding under section 476 of the Code against DW 1 Tajul Islam Chowdhury. 

 60. Mr. Sheikh Muhammed Serajul Islam, learned Advocate for appellant in Criminal Appeal and respondent No.1 in both the Government Appeals submits that the appellant was never given an opportunity to explain the money that was recovered from Senabhaban. If he got such opportunity he could have explained that the money belonged to Jatio Party and there could be no prosecution on this allegation. Mr. Serajul Islam further submits that in course of trial as many as 10 defence witnesses deposed that the Central Committee of Jatio Party decided to purchase its office building and made an application to the Secretary, Ministry of Housing and Public Works. The Ministry made a summary thereon and forwarded it to the Hon'ble President. who approved it and accordingly, the decision was communicated to the rank and file of Jatio Party. Raising fund for that purpose was also proved by very responsible leaders and people's representatives, who gave deposition in full support of the defence case and there was no contradiction between them. This defence case was also proved by proving documents without any objection. Before lodging the FIR, the Acting Secretary General of JP made representation to the Acting President on 05.01.1991 and immediately thereafter instituted a suit for realization of the money. The learned Divisional Special Judge without any cogent ground discarded the defence evidence and most illegally convicted and sentenced the appellant. Besides, the judgment was passed without considering that initiation of the prosecution case was tainted with political motive, which would be further clear from amendment of section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947 just five days before pronouncement of the judgment. Earlier there was no provision of confiscation in the said provision of law, but after framing of charge and before pronouncement of judgment the law was amended and the appellant was sentenced thereunder, which was apparently illegal in view of section 6 of the General Clauses Act. The learned Divisional Special Judge also failed to consider that the claim of money was raised by initiation of a money suit and making a prior representation to the Acting President and fate this criminal case would largely depend on result of the suit. 

 63. Mr. Md. Khurshid Alam Khan, learned Advocate appearing for ACC (respondent 2 in the criminal appeal and co-appellants in Government appeals) submits that under the facts and circumstances of the present case it is crystal clear that the accused-appellant acquired the money in question during his tenure as President. The prosecution case so far it relates to the time of occurrence has also been proved by the evidence of DW 1, who himself' stated that the money was given to the accused-appellant at his office or sometimes at Senabhaban. I he last payment was made to him on 02.12.1990. When the time of occurrence is admitted/proved by the defence itself, there is no scope of raising controversy thereon. 

 64. Mr. Kham further submits that alongside section 5 (2) of the Act 11 of 1947, the Divisional Special Judge was also competent to confiscate any property under section 4(5) of the Act XI, of 1958 and section 517 of the Code. So there was nothing wrong in confiscation of the money and vehicle by the impugned judgment and order. The mentioning of confiscation under the law amended subsequent to lodging the FIR may hardly be considered as an irregularity, which is curable under the law, but when the offence of holding disproportionate property by a person not less than the President is proved beyond all reasonable doubts, he cannot be released or acquitted on a mere irregularity. There was no legal bar in prosecuting the President after his leaving of office. It has been settled by different pronouncements that there is no difficultly in prosecuting a former President, who does not enjoy the immunity anymore under article 51 of the Constitution. In support of his submission Mr. Khan refers to the case of Hussain Mohammad Ershad Vs. State and others 53 DLR 102, affirmed in 21 BLD (AD) 15. 

 65. Mr. Nazibur Rahman, learned Deputy Attorney General appearing for the State submits that usurpation of power by the accused-appellant and attempt to its validation by the Constitution (Seventh Amendment) Act, 1986 having been declared void ab-initio in the case of Siddique Ahmed Vs. Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and others 31 BLD (11CD) 84 (popularly known as seventh amendment case), which has subsequently been affirmed by the Appellate Division in Siddique Ahmed Vs Government of Bangladesh and others 33 BLD (AD) 129 so far it relates to invalidation of the seventh amendment and usurpation of power by the appellant. In such a position the appellant cannot legally be considered as a President and the question of immunity under article 51 on his part does not arise at all. He was a usurper simply and also liable to be prosecuted for violation of the Constitution. So far the merit of the case is concerned learned Deputy Attorney General submits that when such an offence is committed by a person occupying the office of the President, he should be dealt with seriously so that no other ordinary public servant dares to commit such offence endangering the rule of law and accountability of public administration. 

 70. The oft-quoted adage 'the King can do no wrong' is the position in England, and her servants, by analogy cannot be sued for tortious liability, but in our country this adage is not applicable to understand the meaning of article 51 of the Constitution. Even our President is not the Executive Head, which vest in the office of Prime Minister alone under article 55 thereof. It may sound a bit off the subject that in India executive power is vested in the President under article 53 of her Constitution. He is a titular head nevertheless. In England it was the Magna Carta that made the monarch titular head. The Supreme Court of Pakistan in Pakistan through the Secretary, Ministry of Railways and Communications, Karachi Vs. Muhammad A. Hayat 14 DLR (SC) 7 explained that the constitutional status of the Crown wholly, different from that the Government of Pakistan. The Crown of England occupies a unique position. As stated in Dicey's Law of the Constitution (p. 527 of the 1950 Edition), it is fundamental rule of English Law that no action can be brought against the Crown. No process of any kind can he used by the Courts against the Crown. Another recognized principle is that The Crown can do no wrong. The Crown is not responsible fin its act to anybody or authority and no legal right can be said to exist in any person against the Crown." (emphasis supplied) 

 71. None of the above conditions is applicable to our Constitution and an argument based on the equality of Crown's status may be misconceived. The President's immunity in our Constitution under article 51 is available only during his term of office. In the present case, the appellant's trial was commenced after he resigned as President. The constitutional protection under article 51 was no more available to him. On the other hand, he was also holding the office of the executive head, who exercised the executive power of the Republic in a Presidential form of Government that was in force at the material time, and as such he was a public servant liable for prosecution. In the present constitutional scheme, the Prime Minister being head of the executive is a public servant and liable for prosecution even during his tenure in office. It is, therefore, not correct to say that the accused-appellant was immune from prosecution on the analogy of Crown's immunity. 

 77. It is pertinent to mention here that at the time of occurrence, section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947 did not provide any sentence of confiscation. It was amended by Act VIII of 1992 on 29.01.1992 with prospective effect and the sentence of confiscation was added therewith before four days of pronouncement of the impugned judgment. The amended section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947 being a substantive law cannot be applied in sentencing the appellant for an offence which allegedly took place before the amendment reliance placed on Tarique Rahman Vs. Government of Bangladesh represented by the Secretary, Ministry of Law, Justice and Parliamentary Affairs and others 63 DLR (AD) 1621. The sentence of confiscation in the impugned judgment and order is illegal on that count as well. 

 78. The another charge under section 5 (1) (c) of the Act II of 1947 was framed for conversion of the gifts awarded to the President of the Republic for personal use of the appellant, which was scheduled to the Act II of 1947 as well as Act XL of 1958. However, it is already mentioned that possession of disproportionate property by an individual was an offence under section 5 (1) of the Act XXVI of 1957 and was triable by the Anti-Corruption Tribunal constituted under the Ordinance, 1960 not by a Special Judge appointed under the Act XL of 1958. The latter does not provide joinder of charges under two different special laws triable by two different tribunals, except a joint trial of scheduled and non-scheduled offences (meaning the offences triable by ordinary criminal court under the Code of Criminal Procedure) under section 5(7) of the Act XL of 1958 that does not cover the present case. Thus the trial of the present case was inherently illegal for joinder of charges under two different special laws. In this regard we can rely on the case of Talukder Abdul Aziz Vs. The State 35 DLR 127. 

 79. Admittedly the money and vehicle were recovered from the appellant's official residence, but he did not claim it as of his own. The top leaders of Jatio Party deposed as defence witnesses and claimed the money to be of their party, which was not at all credible. The trial Court also discarded their evidences on proper assessment. The then Secretary General in charge of Jatio Party instituted a suit on 07.02.1991 against the Government as well as the appellant for realisation of the money, though did not take steps for disposal of the same. It also does not appear that the appellant being defendant 2 appeared therein and filed any written statement claiming the money as of him. The said suit being renumbered as Money Suit No.334 of 2008 is still pending at the stage of peremptory hearing in the 7th Court of Joint District Judge, Dhaka. It is surprising that despite expiry of 26 (twenty-six) years the suit has not yet been disposed of. 

 83. In Government Appeal No.5 of 1992, we find that the trial Court considered the evidence of PWs 38 and 45 read with exhibits 9/100, 58-62 and material exhibits XIV-XIV/30 and assigned sufficient reasons in acquitting the accused-respondent (appellant in the criminal appeal) of charge under section 5(2) of the Act II of 1947 allegedly for commission of offence under section 5(1) (c) thereof. On sifting the evidence regarding this part of the charges, we also do not find anything wrong in the order of acquittal. This part of the occurrences allegedly took place when the appellant possessed the office of President, but still the trial so far it relates to the charge under the said provision was illegal for misjoinder of charges triable under two different special laws by two different Tribunals. When the trial itself was illegal for misjoinder of charges, the question of enhancement of sentence or awarding that under section 5(2) for commission of offence under section 5(1) (c) of the Act on setting aside the acquittal does not arise. We thus do not find any merit in Government Appeal No.5 of 1992. 

 84. It is already mentioned that Jatio Party had claimed the money in question by making a representation to the Acting President on 05.01.1991 (exhibit-Jha) i.e. before lodgment of the FIR and subsequently by instituting a suit on 07.02.1991, before framing of charge in the criminal case. The suit is still pending and the factum of raising party-fund by way of selling money receipts and collection of members' subscriptions have been pleaded in the plaint of the suit (exhbit-Ttha) in the same way of defence as taken in the instant criminal case. In such a position, whether the DW 1 Tajul Islam Chowdhury should be prosecuted under section 195(c) read with section 476 of the Code for recording/adducing false evidence or not, would depend on the nature of evidence that is going to be led in the suit and its final result. At this stage it would be an overstepping, if the Government Appeal No.6 of 1992 is allowed. It may also prejudge the suit already pending before a competent civil court. This Court thus restrains itself from giving any decision on this point despite the trial court passed a non-speaking order in rejecting the application of the Public Prosecutor and held in its judgment that the constitution of Jatio Party (exhibit-Da) was subsequently created for the purpose of the case, and that the money receipts (exhibits-Gha and Ta series) were not genuine and that the register (exhibit-GO was not acceptable. The civil court will be competent to initiate such case, if any, only after disposal of the suit. In this regard, we should also keep in mind that the gravity of offence regarding perjury/false evidence in a criminal case is always lesser than that of a case of civil nature. 

 85. Accordingly, the Criminal Appeal No. 173 of 1992 is allowed, Government Appeal No.5 of 1992 is dismissed and Government Appeal No.6 of 1992 is dismissed with the above observation. The impugned judgment and order dated 03.02.1992 passed by the Divisional Special Judge, Dhaka in Special Case No. 7 of 1991 convicting and sentencing the appellant under section 5 (2) read with section 5 (1) (e) of the Act II of 1947 is set aside. The appellant is acquitted of the charge. In spite of setting aside the impugned judgment and order, the money and vehicle will not go back to the appellant (Hussain Mohammad Ershad). Those being unclaimed shall vest in the Government under article 143 (3) of the Constitution subject to decision of the suit.
